title: Compiler error, or linker error?

prereqs.why: Which tool complains depends entirely on whether the missing thing is a declaration or a definition.
The examples are all functions, and what a function declaration does and does not provide is the question.
One of the cases is about what putting a definition in a header does.

statement:
A program in two files. `main.cpp` includes `maths.h` and calls functions from it; `maths.cpp` is meant to define them.

Knowing which tool will complain — the compiler or the linker — tells you where to look, and it is the single most useful thing to be able to predict about a build failure.

**Which of these statements are true?** Select all that apply.
hints: The compiler sees one translation unit at a time and never looks at another `.cpp`. So what can it possibly know about whether a function body exists?
A declaration is a promise that something exists somewhere. Who checks that the promise was kept, and when?
One of these is about `inline`, which exists precisely to make an exception to the one-definition rule.

options: If `maths.h` declares `int square(int);` and no `.cpp` ever defines it, `main.cpp` compiles successfully and the **linker** reports an undefined reference.
If `main.cpp` calls `square(2, 3)` with two arguments while the header declares it taking one, the **compiler** reports the error.
If a non-inline function is *defined* in `maths.h` and the header is included by two different `.cpp` files, the **linker** reports a duplicate definition.
Adding `inline` to a function defined in a header makes the duplicate-definition problem go away, because an inline function may be defined in every translation unit that uses it.
